https://english.radio.cz/voice-was-meant.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК The voice that was meant to conquer the airwaves: How Radio Prague spread communist propaganda (4) Facebook Twitter The voice that was meant to conquer the airwaves: How Radio Prague spread communism around the world (4) 27:33 ⨯ The voice that was meant to conquer the airwaves: How Radio Prague spread communism around the world (4) https://english.radio.cz/voice-was-meant-conquer-airwaves-how-radio-prague-spread-communist-propaganda-4-8889752#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X Apple iTunes YouTube Music Spotify RSS feed - other readers During the communist era Radio Prague functioned as a highly effective Cold War propaganda tool, tailoring communist messaging to audiences around the world, while operating under strict censorship and centralized control. Yet amid the ideological campaigns and bureaucratic machinery, occasional human moments and the haunting sound of a Slovak fujara closing the day's broadcast offered rare glimpses of authenticity behind the propaganda. The crackle of radio waves, tuning to the right frequency, and a familiar voice from afar speaking to listeners somewhere across the ocean. At a time when the world was divided by the Iron Curtain, it was not only ordinary news from home that was broadcast from Prague studios over the air. Radio waves became a sophisticated weapon in the ideological war. Although Czech Radio’s international service was ostensibly meant to inform the world about developments in Czechoslovakia, its principal hidden—and often explicit—mission was singular: to systematically spread the ideas of communism and convince the planet of the superiority of socialism. It should be added that, from a professional standpoint, the station carried out this gigantic propaganda task with remarkable flexibility and success. A double face for America and Africa’s awakening Prague adopted an exceptionally sophisticated approach toward the United States, where, paradoxically, it directed two different broadcasts. While moderate programs drew on nostalgia and appealed to Czech and Slovak Americans with the greeting “Dear compatriots, your old homeland is calling you,” the broader American audience was targeted with sharp propaganda. The broadcasts did not hesitate to exploit issues such as nuclear testing, describing it as a huge business from which American shareholders reaped enormous dividends. The height of emotional manipulation came in a program marking the anniversary of the bombing of Hiroshima, in which chilling voices warned American mothers that humanity no longer measured the lines of life on the palm of the hand, but rather the deadly Strontium-90 in the bones of future generations. As colonial empires began to collapse at the turn of the 1950s and 1960s, the attention of Prague’s strategists shifted toward Africa. The aim was to draw newly independent states into the socialist camp. Broadcasts in English, French, and Swahili began to fill the airwaves. Although the official rhetoric thundered about supporting the struggle against imperialism and grandly addressed African listeners as “the voice of friendship from Prague,” the day-to-day reality in the newsroom was often a matter of exhausting routine. Former editor of the French-language service Alena Gebertová recalls the work of the time without illusions: “All of it came from the central authorities. They were mandatory, dry reports saying that one First Secretary had departed and another had arrived.” Reflecting on what listeners on the African savannahs might have found engaging in such sterile content, Gebertová adds that, in the political climate of the era, the mere fact that the unknown Central European country speaking to them was communist undoubtedly played an important role. Into the heart of dictatorships from secret villas Yet Czechoslovak radio waves also penetrated far more dangerous territory—directly into the heart of countries gripped by right-wing dictatorships. In General Franco’s fascist Spain, Radio Prague’s reports on miners’ strikes became highly sought-after material subject to the strictest censorship. “If someone was caught listening to Radio Prague in Spanish back then, things got bad very quickly,” recalls Antonio Casado, a member of the Spanish-language editorial team. According to him, the regime immediately branded such listening as incitement to subvert the state. A similarly significant role was played by the newsroom broadcasting to Pinochet’s Chile. Chilean journalists in exile working in Prague hosted a program called Chile Will Triumph, obtaining exclusive information from their homeland through teleprinters supplied by the Cuban news agency Prensa Latina. An even more clandestine, almost espionage-like dimension characterized the broadcast known as Rome 2, which from 1950 onward pretended to be transmitting directly from Italy. Researcher Ulrico Bovo reveals the secret of those involved: “They were Italian partisans who had legal troubles back home. Here they received false documents, new identities, and broadcast from concealed apartments in Prague.” The illusion of a free local radio station was so convincing that during violent street demonstrations in Italy, people called the Prague newsroom directly from public phone booths to advise fellow protesters live on air about routes of escape from police cordons. Czechoslovakia responded with similar speed in 1981, when it rapidly launched broadcasts aimed at Poland, then shaken by the Solidarity trade union movement, with the stated goal of providing “a personal example of the achievements of real socialism.” Folders, stamps, and the melancholic sound of the fujara This global propaganda colossus, however, could not have produced a single report without a flawlessly lubricated censorship machine. Editors themselves had virtually no freedom; they merely translated texts issued by the central newsroom. Everything had to pass through an official censorship apparatus. Typed pages were placed into protective folders affectionately nicknamed “shirts,” and the editor would carry them to the respective glass partition. Only when a vigilant censor stamped the folder with an official seal could the words be sent into the airwaves. Renowned journalist Pavla Jazairiová looks back on her years in the African editorial department with sober hindsight. She acknowledges that it was pure propaganda, yet even there occasional openings for ordinary human warmth could be found. “A Senegalese listener once wrote to us that Christmas is celebrated in palaces and huts alike. And imagine—it got through,” she recalls with a mischievous smile. The absurdity of the entire approval and censorship apparatus reached a tragicomic climax during the August invasion of 1968. Karel Wichs describes the chilling moment when the besieged radio building came under fire while the management desperately tried to maintain the appearance of normal operations. “The director calmly told us that they were only using blank cartridges. And at that exact moment, the ceiling collapsed on top of us,” Wichs recounts, describing the bizarre final act in the illusion of controlled airwaves. Yet whether those carefully censored folders were destined for left-wing intellectuals in Chile, miners in Andalusia, or farmers in the American Midwest, Radio Prague’s broadcasts always contained one unique and warm element. As the forceful political slogans faded away and the work shift neared its end, Slovak editor Jožka Rybár would take the microphone. With characteristic grace, he would set aside all prescribed directives and pick up a traditional wooden fujara. Its melancholy yet profoundly human sound would travel out into the world, a fleeting expression of pure beauty marking the end of each day beneath the vast ideological machinery of communist propaganda. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Sisters Mariangela Marras, 99, and Giovanna Marras (101) at home in Balotana, Sardinia. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian Italy Is sisterhood the secret to a long life? The Sardinian village that could hold key to women’s longevity Meet some of the elderly residents of Bolotana, in line to be the world’s sixth ‘blue zone’ for its high number of female centenarians Angela Giuffrida in Bolotana Sun 18 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen Giovanna Marras opens the door to her home in Bolotana, a mountain village in central Sardinia, her eyes are bright with curiosity as she sizes up her visitors. Her sister, Mariangela, peeks out too, soon ushering her guests inside and handing out dishes of ice-cream. The sisters are full of life, talking animatedly. Giovanna is 101 and Mariangela is 99. Sitting in their living room, Giovanna swiftly recaps her life story: she excelled at school before moving to Cagliari, the capital of the Italian island, at 18 to train as a seamstress. The sisters went on to run a successful tailoring business in Bolotana before travelling the world after retirement. Neither married. View image in fullscreen Giovanna and Mariangela Marras when they were younger. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian “Someone did come to the house and ask my parents for my hand in marriage,” Giovanna said. “I told them to tell him to go away – I mean, a woman should at least know her future husband.” Mariangela is equally as feisty in her response. “I didn’t want to get married … I walk my own path, I don’t need support.” The details of their lives are now being examined as part of a broader pattern of exceptional longevity in Bolotana , where women are driving a trend that could put the village, population 2,266, in the running to be the world’s sixth “blue zone” – geographic areas with unusually high concentrations of centenarians. Sardinia was home to the first such zone , identified more than 25 years ago. A study by professors at the University of Sassari and the University of Alabama at Birmingham in the US, published in the scientific journal Frontiers in Aging last week, found that 13.8% of women in Bolotana who reach the age of 70 will live to 100 – placing it second in the world for female longevity after Hong Kong. Giovanna is the third eldest of six female centenarians in Bolotana, after Tonia Giglio and Maddalena Falchi, both 102. By the end of this year, two other women are expected to reach the milestone, and in 2027 two more, including Mariangela. The last male centenarian, Giovanni Madau, died in July, a few months short of his 102nd birthday. Tore Pedde, the president of Orminas , a cultural association, played a crucial role in uncovering Bolotana as a potential longevity hotspot after painstakingly searching its demographic archives, even tracking down centenarians born in the village who had long since moved overseas. Records of people born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925 showed that 38 had lived beyond 100, putting their longevity rate at 57% higher than the Italian national average. View image in fullscreen Tore Pedde helped uncover Bolotana as a potential longevity hotspot. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian “Up until the early 1900s, Bolotana followed a trend whereby men significantly outnumbered women among the elderly,” Pedde said. “From the early 20th century onwards, however, the trend shifted and women began to outnumber men. Later, the number of female centenarians started to far exceed the male ones, and this trend continues today.” While it has already been well established that women live longer for biological reasons, scientists behind the study are tracing family trees in search of genetic clues to Bolotana’s female longevity. They are also exploring the roles of diet, physical activity and social connections. View image in fullscreen Filomena Scarpa is a former language teacher who turned 100 in January. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian A striking characteristic of Bolotana’s female centenarians is their independence. The Marras sisters still cook for themselves, eating a varied but clean diet without forsaking meat, cheese or wine. Mariangela does the shopping, which entails a walk down a hilly street and back. The women have grit and are remarkably lucid. Filomena Scarpa, a former language teacher who turned 100 in January, began learning German in her 90s and was a voracious reader before a problem with her left eye started to hinder her. “It saddens me not to be able to read with the same level of consistency,” she said. She goes to a personal trainer twice a week. “Because I can’t sit around all day.” Scarpa, who has two sons, is a childhood friend of Falchi, who now lives with her daughter about an hour away in Oristana. The pair speak often. Falchi is notorious in Bolotana for smoking like a trooper. “I told her to quit because it’s not good for her health,” Scarpa said. “But she said: ‘It hasn’t got me so far, so I shall carry on.’” Bolotana is situated in Sardinia’s Marghine mountains, about 70 miles (110km) from the island’s original blue zone – a cluster of villages nestled on the slopes of the central and eastern provinces. View image in fullscreen Francesco Manconi, the mayor of Bolotana, believes ‘the abundance of natural affection’ helps the town’s citizens live to a great age. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian “What’s special here is that for the first time we’ve identified an area where women live to a great age, whereas the original blue zone was predominantly male,” said Giovanni Mario Pes, who led the study and is a co-creator of the blue zone concept. “We therefore need to explain why longevity specifically affects women here.” Unlike the original villages, Bolotana is relatively close to cities, including Sassari and Alghero on the west coast. Still, its streets are steep, providing residents with unavoidable exercise. The environment is unspoiled and most people still eat fruit and vegetables grown in their gardens. One thing Pes noted among its female residents was a “strong sense of sisterhood”. “This felt quite unusual and is something I’d like to explore scientifically,” he added. View image in fullscreen Bolotana is situated in Sardinia’s Marghine mountains, about 70 miles from the island’s original blue zone. Photograph: Victor Sokolowicz/The Guardian Francesco Manconi, the mayor of Bolotana, believes the sociality is key. “There is an abundance of natural affection, whether from family members, neighbours or friends, towards our elderly,” he said, adding that the village placed “a great importance” on ensuring they could stay in their own homes. Betti Uda, who runs a tourism business, said the village’s elderly women were determined and still tried to live purposefully. “If they want to do something, they will – nothing holds them back.” Explore more on these topics Italy Life expectancy Older people Ageing Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
